summary.text: A 57-year-old woman presented on June 19, 2019 seeking relief from tinnitus and hearing loss, with a history of severe sinusitis, insomnia, fatigue and stress and normal vital signs. One year earlier she had developed left ear fullness, high pitch ringing and vertigo, then a very loud high-pitch noise with left hearing loss at SUD 8/10 and sleep interruption.

An ENT audiogram showed significant left ear hearing loss of 40 dB within 250 to 4,000 Hz. A main Neuropuncture tinnitus prescription was given at the first treatment, and hearing began to return. After 3 treatments she heard a different layer of sound, and 12 treatments twice a week with Main and Modified Protocols were conducted.

She reported ear draining and the ringing becoming lower and less intense at SUD 4/10, and her relationship with her husband improved. At the ENT 1 year follow-up in June 2020 the audiology test showed significant improvement in left ear hearing; at eighteen months tinnitus was occasionally noticeable, SUD was 1/10 and hearing continued to improve.

summary.text: A 54-year-old woman presented on July 21, 2020 reporting complete loss of hearing in the left ear, with normal vital signs. Her history included tinnitus with low-pitch roaring at SUD 6/10, insomnia, headaches, blurry vision with nystagmus, severe sinus congestion, neck pain and hot flashes. Hearing loss followed her fourth craniectomy for recurrent posterior fossa ependymoma, and she was diagnosed with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss.

Before the first Neuropuncture treatment she could not hear finger clicks outside the left ear; the tinnitus main protocol was used at the first session and afterward she regained some hearing. Sinus congestion was much reduced after the second treatment, and after the third she could hear conversation close to the left ear, with roaring reduced to SUD 2/10.

An audiogram on August 21, 2020, after 9 treatments including Tinnitus Main and Modified Protocols, showed she could hear from 500 to 2,000 Hz at 20 dB in the left ear, with poor low- and high-pitch hearing, which was better than the complete loss of hearing in July 2020.

summary.text: A 52-year-old man presented on July 2, 2020 with tinnitus and fullness in his right ear and normal vital signs. He had felt fluid in the right ear in 2004 and an ear tube was implanted, removed in 2012; tinnitus began in 2016 and a hole in the ear drum was found in 2018. The ringing was at SUD 6/10.

In June 2020 the ENT doctor suggested inserting another ear tube and prescribed steroid medicine, but the patient decided to pursue the acupuncture route. After the first Neuropuncture tinnitus prescription treatment he reported immediate relief with reduced right ear fullness, and the SUD scale dropped from 6/10 to 4/10.

The Neuropuncture treatment plan was 6 weeks for a total of 12 treatments including Tinnitus Main and Modified protocols. At the end of the plan on September 24, 2020 he reported tinnitus reduced to SUD 1/10 with only a slight sloshing/flapping sound once or twice a day.

article_limitations: Table 2 summarizes 14 patients, three of whom are described in detail as Case 1 to Case 3, but the article never says which rows correspond to which case; ages differ for two plausible matches (57 vs 59 and 52 vs 56). The 14 table rows are therefore not extracted as patient facts and only p1 to p3 are in the roster.
Table 2 has no per-patient serial measurements (one row per patient with a single follow-up result), so no measurement series was built.
The Discussion sentence restating each case in a phrase ("long-term severe sinusitis", "puncture to the eardrum") adds wording not present in the case sections and was not extracted as facts.

The shared treatment description (points, devices, 25 Hz microcurrent and 2 Hz millicurrent dosage, Table 1) is general methodology and was not assigned to individual patients; case text names only "Tinnitus Main and Modified Protocols".
Caption-layer visual status is not_inspected; actual images are inspected in separate visual targets.
Study-level claims of effectiveness in the Abstract and Conclusion are not copied to individual patients.

Roster: the article states 14 patients in Table 2 and that three of them are described in detail; only Cases 1 to 3 are individuated with narrative courses, so the roster holds p1 to p3 (reported 14, roster incomplete). The other 11 rows cannot be separated from the three detailed cases without attribute matching, so they are not rostered as separate patients.

Figures 1 to 4 are photographs of a person used to illustrate treatment points; the article does not say who is photographed and ties no image to a case. Side-view faces are visible in Figures 1 and 3 and are flagged in the privacy sidecar.
